challenges.title: An interesting shadow
challenges.description: Find and photograph a shadow you like, wherever you are.
tips: Shadows are longest and most graphic early and late in the day.
Frame the shadow itself, not the object casting it.
Shoot straight down at the ground for a more abstract result.

challenges.title: An overlooked detail
challenges.description: Photograph a detail you never usually notice, somewhere familiar.
tips: Pick a room you walk through every day without ever looking at it.
Crouch down or look up: overlooked things are rarely at eye level.
Handles, switches, wall corners: the mundane makes good photos.

challenges.title: A close-up texture
challenges.description: Get as close as you can to a surface that intrigues you and capture its texture.
tips: Move in until the focus gives up, then back off slightly.
Raking light brings out texture far better than light from the front.
Fill the whole frame, leave no background visible.

challenges.title: Something red
challenges.description: Go on the hunt for something red and photograph it.
tips: Red pops much harder against a neutral or dark background.
Don't hunt for a big object, a red detail is enough.
If you can't find any, walk outside for five minutes, you'll see it everywhere.

challenges.title: An unexpected reflection
challenges.description: Find an unusual reflective surface (shop window, spoon, puddle) and photograph your reflection.
tips: Puddles after rain give the most surprising reflections.
You don't need to be sharp or recognisable in the reflection.
Look for curved surfaces, they distort and make the image intriguing.

challenges.title: An unusual angle
challenges.description: Pick an everyday object and photograph it from an angle you never use.
tips: Put the object on the floor and shoot it from directly above.
Or the opposite: phone flat on the ground, shooting upward.
Try three different angles before you pick one.

challenges.title: The light right now
challenges.description: Photograph the light exactly as it is right now, indoors or outside.
tips: Photograph the light, not what it lights: look for a patch, a shaft.
Don't correct the exposure, keep the mood exactly as it is.
A window, a curtain or a wall is subject enough.

challenges.title: Intentional blur
challenges.description: Photograph a moving scene, letting the blur happen on purpose.
tips: Move the phone slightly as the shutter fires.
A subject passing in front of a still background gives the nicest effect.
Take several, a good blur is partly down to luck.

challenges.title: A repeating pattern
challenges.description: Spot a pattern or repetition (tiles, windows, leaves) and photograph it.
tips: Keep the frame parallel to the pattern to strengthen the repetition.
Cut the pattern at the edge of the frame, it suggests it carries on.
Stairs, railings, facades and shelves are reliable bets.

challenges.title: Whatever makes you smile
challenges.description: Photograph the first thing that makes you smile today.
tips: Don't overthink it, the first thing that makes you smile is the right one.
It can be tiny or ordinary, nobody's judging.
Shoot it right away, before the moment passes.

challenges.title: The sky between things
challenges.description: Look up and photograph the sky framed by whatever surrounds it: branches, rooftops, power lines.
tips: Grey days work very well: the sky becomes a plain backdrop.
Frame it so the sky fills at least half the image.
From a window works too, if you're staying in.

challenges.title: Backlit
challenges.description: Position yourself so the light is behind your subject, then photograph it.
tips: A window during the day is enough: put the object between it and you.
Your subject will go dark, almost a silhouette. That's the point.
Tap the bright area on screen to darken the silhouette even more.

challenges.title: Your meal as it is
challenges.description: Photograph what you're eating today, without moving or arranging anything.
tips: Take it before you start eating, or it's lost already.
Straight down from above is the simplest framing.
The table, your hands, the mess around it are part of the picture.

challenges.title: An improvised still life
challenges.description: Gather three objects within arm's reach and photograph them together.
tips: They don't need to have anything in common. The arrangement is enough.
Put them near a window and let daylight do the work.
Move one of them and shoot again: keep the one you prefer.

challenges.title: An empty space
challenges.description: Photograph somewhere empty: an unoccupied chair, a corridor, a deserted street.
tips: Emptiness shows best where you'd expect someone to be.
Step back: the more space around it, the stronger it feels.
Early in the morning, almost everything is empty.

challenges.title: Someone's trace
challenges.description: Photograph a sign that someone has been there: a cup left out, shoes by the door, an unmade bed.
tips: Don't tidy anything first: the mess is what tells the story.
Get close, one object is enough.
Your own traces count too.

challenges.title: Catching movement
challenges.description: Photograph something in motion, this time trying to keep it sharp.
tips: The more light there is, the easier it gets: outdoors or near a window.
Tap several times in a row and keep the best one.
A falling object, a moving hand, an animal: start simple.

challenges.title: A well-worn object
challenges.description: Photograph something you use every day that carries the marks of use.
tips: Wear and tear shows up better close in.
A chopping board, keys, a pair of shoes.
Turn the object until you find its most battered side.

challenges.title: Without looking at the screen
challenges.description: Take a photo without looking at the screen: hold out your arm, aim by instinct, press.
tips: Hold the phone at hip height for an unusual viewpoint.
Take several in a row, keep the one that surprises you.
A crooked frame is part of the result.

challenges.title: A light in the dim
challenges.description: Find a dim spot, a room with the curtains closed, a hallway, a half-open closet, and photograph a light source that's on: a lamp, a screen, a night light.
tips: No need to wait for night: a room with the shutters closed or a closed closet works fine.
Turn off the other lights around so the source stands out.
Tap the light on screen so everything else goes properly dark.
